title: Swiss Physicists Fire 'Atomic Cannon' to Test Einstein's Gravity Rule
excerpt: Researchers at ETH Zurich and the Paul Scherrer Institute have produced an intense, precisely controlled beam of muonium atoms — opening the first path to measuring gravity's pull on second-generation matter.
body:
• Physicists at ETH Zurich and the Paul Scherrer Institute have produced an intense, highly controlled beam of muonium atoms, reporting the advance in Nature Physics.
  • Muonium — an electron bound to a positively charged antimuon — is the first system dominated by second-generation matter that can be shaped into a beam precise enough for a gravity experiment.
  • The gravity measurement has not yet been made; the new beam opens a path to measuring muonium's free fall to about 1% precision within roughly 100 days of data collection.

Physicists in Switzerland have built what amounts to an atomic cannon — a beam of exotic muonium atoms so tightly controlled that it could soon reveal whether Einstein's rule that everything falls at the same rate holds for a type of matter never before put to the test.

The advance, reported in Nature Physics, comes from researchers at ETH Zurich and the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen. They produced muonium inside superfluid helium cooled to about 0.2 kelvin, and the quantum liquid expelled the atoms vertically into vacuum at nearly identical speeds — creating the controlled beam an atom-interference experiment needs.

"We have taken an important step toward carrying out an exciting experiment on this topic. We want to measure the gravitational interaction of the muon."

— Anna Soter, professor of physics, ETH Zurich

Context & Background

Since Galileo, physicists have confirmed that objects fall with the same acceleration regardless of their composition. Einstein elevated that universality of free fall — the weak equivalence principle — into a foundational pillar of general relativity, and scientists have since tested it with ordinary matter to extraordinary precision, and more recently with antimatter.

One corner of the particle world has remained out of reach. Ordinary matter is made of first-generation particles — up and down quarks and electrons. Nature also has second and third generations: heavier, unstable cousins that decay rapidly into first-generation particles. The muon is the electron's heavier sibling from the second generation, decaying within about 2.2 microseconds. No one has ever directly measured how gravity acts on matter dominated by such a particle.

Muonium is the ideal probe. It resembles a hydrogen atom, but its nucleus holds no proton — instead a positively charged antimuon, paired with an ordinary electron. It is electrically neutral, which matters because gravity is so weak that stray electromagnetic fields would overwhelm the measurement for a charged particle. The catch is its lifetime: muonium survives only about two millionths of a second before decaying, far too briefly for the diffuse beams of earlier attempts.

Impact & Analysis

The team's method clears that barrier. Anti-muons from PSI's particle accelerator are stopped in a two-millimeter layer of liquid helium chilled nearly to absolute zero, where they capture electrons and form muonium. The positive chemical potential of muonium in the superfluid then acts as an "atomic cannon," propelling the newly formed atoms vertically upward with consistent speeds and directions.

The result is what the researchers call a superthermal muonium beam: unusually strong and unusually orderly, with atoms clustered tightly around a single speed of about 2,180 meters per second, and roughly 8% of stopped anti-muons converting into usable muonium. No muonium beam this narrow has ever existed.

The experiment was carried out at PSI's CHRISP particle-physics facility, with doctoral students Robert Waddy, Jesse Zhang and Paul Wegmann aligning the apparatus. The team has not yet measured muonium's gravitational acceleration. Its planned atom-interferometry experiment could become the first direct test of whether the weak equivalence principle applies to second-generation matter — and a measured deviation would point to the existence of a further, as-yet-unknown fundamental force.

What's Next

The team projects its beam could measure muonium's gravitational acceleration to about 1% precision within roughly 100 days of data collection. If the atoms fall exactly as Einstein predicts, the result extends the equivalence principle into a new domain. If they do not, physicists get the first experimental hint of physics beyond the current picture — and a race to build more precise instruments to chase it.
